INDEPENDENT
Independent of the usual axioms of set theory (ZFC).
For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ let $A_x\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded set with outer measure $<1$. 
Must there exist an infinite independent set, that is, some infinite $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $x\not\in A_y$ for all $x\neq y\in X$?
If the sets $A_x$ are closed and have measure $<1$, then must there exist an independent set of size $3$?
#501: [Er61][ErHa71]
combinatorics | 
set theory
Under the assumptions of the second question, Gladysz [Gl62] proved the existence of an independent set of size $2$, and Newelski, Pawlikowski, and Seredyński [NPS87] proved the existence of an infinite independent set, giving a strong affirmative answer to the second question.
For the first question:
 Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa60] proved the existence of arbitrarily large finite independent sets.
 Hechler [He72] proved the answer is no, assuming the continuum hypothesis.
Newelski, Pawlikowski, and Seredyński [NPS87] proved the answer is yes under the stronger assumption that all $A_x$ are closed.
 Lee proved the answer is yes, assuming the existence of an extension of the Lebesgue measure to all subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.
 Glazer (using GPT 5.6 Sol, Fable 5, and Opus 4.8) proved the answer to the first question is independent of ZFC.
Additional thanks to: Boris Alexeev

 I have written a short note on this problem: GitHub repository
With the assistance of GPT-5.5 Pro, I found a proof of a relative independence result. Assuming that Lebesgue measure extends to a countably additive measure on all subsets of the real line, the answer is positive: every family $(A_y)_{y\in\mathbb R}$ with $m^*(A_y)< 1$ admits an infinite independent set.
The proof uses Fremlin's Theorem 543C, a Fubini-type inequality attributed there to a 1970 note of Kunen.
I have checked the argument myself, but I am not an expert in this area. Comments, corrections, and references to related work would be very welcome.

 A total extension of Lebesgue measure exists iff there is a real-valued measurable cardinal $\le \mathfrak{c}.$ This has large cardinal strength, but it is usually routine to transfer the combinatorial consequences of this axiom to the extension of any CH model by \omega_2 random reals. I tasked Sol with this transfer and it seems to have succeeded. Here is the chat and here is the draft.
I have vetted neither this argument nor Sungchul's. Instead, I will offer up this draft as a good autoformalization candidate. The proof is factored into 6 components, the first three of which (F1-F3) can be done in parallel with no preparatory work. F4-F6 is the forcing analysis. To get that off the ground, one would need to redo Flypitch in Lean 4 but with the $\omega_2$-random algebra $\mathbb{B}_{\omega_2}$ instead of the $\omega_2$-Cohen algebra.
Then formalize Hechler's negative resolution under CH to get independence of the first component of this problem, and finally formalize [NPS87] to handle the second component of this problem.

A full proof 
claimed by Elliot Glazer (using GPT5.6 Sol, Fable 5, Opus 4.8).
 Summary:
 Result: the first question is independent of ZFC, with both truth values being relatively consistent with ZFC. The second question has a positive resolution. All are formalized in Lean and checked by Comparator.
Ideas: This problem had already been mostly resolved, with Newelski-Pawlikowski-Seredyński having already positively resolved the second question, Hechler having shown consistency of a negative resolution of the first, and Sungchul Lee having shown a positive resolution of the first follows from a real-valued measurable (RVM) cardinal (which is equiconsistent with a measurable cardinal). It only remained to drop the large cardinal hypothesis. It is routine to transfer reasonably combinatorial \Pi^2_1 consequences of an RVM to the extension of an arbitrary CH model by \omega_2 random reals, so we applied the standard technology of this conversion. This confirms neither truth value adds consistency strength.
